referred_to_by.content: A visual anchor for the project: art, price, reform, and institutional display held together as one unstable field.

The work exists as an object, and the image published here is a photograph of it. The studio states, on 2026-09-22, that Art Market Reform exists and is held in its own collection, and that the file published with this record is a photograph of that physical work rather than a born-digital image. That is the studio's statement about its own holdings, recorded as such; nobody outside the studio has examined the object, and no measurement, medium, support or date of making is recorded here because none has been supplied. Two consequences should be read off it. The first is that this record's modelling is provisional and known to be incomplete: it types the work as a digital object classified as a digital image, which describes the photograph and not the thing photographed, and a fuller record would describe the object and treat this file as documentation of it. That correction is deferred until the object's particulars are to hand, and is noted here so that a reader does not take the present typing for a considered claim about what the work is. The second is that the photograph's own date is not established: the file as published carries no camera metadata, having been re-encoded, so it dates neither the object nor the photographing.

A second painting carries this title, and it is the one the studio put on its website. The Internet Archive's capture of the studio's site on 2014-12-18, and again on 2016-01-11, carries a photograph of a painting lettered 'ART MARKET REFORM' across a blue ground worked with white. That is not the painting photographed for this record, which sets the words over a dense multicoloured ground with 'Art' in block letters and 'Market Reform' in script. Two paintings therefore share the title, and the one a third party dates is not the one published here. The consequence for this record is that its subject is ambiguous as it stands: it names a title, publishes a photograph of one object, and does not say which object the title's other uses in this collection refer to. A fuller record should describe a set and say which painting each statement is about.

A website for the work, 2014. In public Facebook comments of 2014-02-05 and 2014-05-09, at times Facebook assigns, the studio linked artmarketreform.com as the work's site, the second reading '"Art Market Reform" is #Metaconceptual #Art and looks like this: http://artmarketreform.com/'. No capture of that site from 2014 exists, so what it showed then is not known. The earliest capture, of 2016-05-09, shows a blog titled 'Art Market Reform' with a single post, 'History of the Art Market', a dated compilation of press reports on the art market's opacity and taxation, which the studio states in 2026 was its own; the comments are set out in the archived-websites record. The studio's Twitter account @ArtMarketReform, linking to that site, was created on the same day, 2016-05-09, by Twitter's own record; it too is set out in the archived-websites record. Later statements, recorded for continuity and not for dating. The studio principal's Facebook account went on presenting Art Market Reform as a work: two photographs described as 'Art Market Reform' were added to an album titled 'Art Works' on 2019-11-22; a post of 2019-12-07, written in the week Maurizio Cattelan's 'Comedian', a banana taped to a wall, was sold at an art fair, says he hopes people 'don't forget that I was working on an art work titled "Art Market Reform"' 'over 7 years ago', a comparison that is the studio's own and is not adopted here; a comment of 2019-12-09 describes it as 'Art Market Reform: To promote Transparency, Accountability, and Responsibility in The Art Market.'; a post of 2021-05-02 offers at auction 'my first NFT', 'just an original digital photograph of the artwork' and not the work itself; a post of 2022-04-05, as recorded among the account's post edits, calls it 'my little long running art project titled "Art Market Reform"'; and a post of 2023-10-03 presents AI-generated billboard versions of 'my human made art work "Art Market Reform" from 2013'. All are the studio's own statements at dates Facebook assigns, in the account data it delivered on 2026-09-24 (the posts file of 4,040,719 bytes, SHA-256 e4008f3e3b6a790a532c26b94eabe6b28314671c04fd2370c410d472a7228db2; the post-edits file of 2,236,144 bytes, SHA-256 6eac1803ac65c6ee0efb06b4e1f97cc722c4de5289a587e21ea927e1174dcf46; the album file of 11,019 bytes, SHA-256 824986f85540e9fb82c099c974a8b85695bb5a7c25d37ccae622ada2ee6f18b1; and the comments file, SHA-256 6bccd7fe8c5e3057c9fccbdcffa62519501e3e8c3585eaccd09eb914ca5249d0, within the archive of SHA-256 c978c3bd338a6a9a934d3aa05a81d2c298c49200bf7e4edc98b8329c02103097). They add no earlier date. Their own datings of the work, 'over 7 years' before December 2019 and 'from 2013', sit with the public comment of 2012-08-14, 'Coming Soon: Art Market Reform ! ! !', and with the message of 2013-05-29 calling it one of his 'more recent works'. Whether the NFT was minted, and where, was not checked.

Named, and called a title, in a letter to a museum on 2013-09-12. The studio's letter to the Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art introduces two works by name: 'Two popular examples of Metaconceptual Art, which are ongoing through time and space as well, are titled "Art Market Reform" , and "Art Tax"'. It then glosses this one: 'Promoting Art Tax on the local, state, national, and international levels to encourage and promote accountability, transparency, and regulation in the Art Market and Art World.' That is the earliest naming of this work delivered to an institution, though not the earliest dated: a public Facebook comment of 2012-08-14 reads 'Coming Soon: Art Market Reform ! ! !', and a private message of 2013-05-29 calls it one of the writer's more recent works of Metaconceptual Art, both set out in the record of the 2012-2013 Facebook and USA Projects evidence; it is in the artist's own words, and it was delivered to a named institution which produced its own copy from its archive in 2026, so the date does not rest on the studio's mailbox alone. Three limits go with it. The letter attests that the title was in use on that date; it does not date the making of the image published with this record, and its own phrase, that the works are 'ongoing through time and space', describes them as continuing rather than finished. The letter attaches images but names none of them, so nothing in it identifies the file published here as the thing it names. And a title used in 2013 says nothing about 2009 or before.
